headline.main: Merz Under Fire: German Conservatives Roiled by Chancellor's Decision on Arms for Israel
headline.social: Merz Under Fire: German Conservatives Roiled by Chancellor's Decision on Arms for Israel

intro: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz decided last week to partially suspend arms deliveries to Israel - a policy shift he made all on his own. Conservative lawmakers in the country are furious.
text:
Let’s assume for a moment that it is true what the confidant of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is saying over the phone. It is the confidant’s own personal interpretation; it doesn’t necessarily have to reflect the views of the chancellor. But he has known Merz for a long time and believes he knows how the chancellor ticks. If his assessment is correct, then the great commotion surrounding Merz’s recent decision on Germany’s Israel policy comes down to a single, simple question.
On Thursday night, the Israeli Security Cabinet agreed to further escalate military operations in the Gaza Strip and to take control of Gaza City. Just a few hours later, at 12:10 p.m. on Friday, the Chancellery responded. In a brief press statement, Merz announced that "under these circumstances,” the German government would no longer approve for the foreseeable future arms exports "that could be deployed in the Gaza Strip.”
Was the chancellor at all aware what this shift in Germany’s Israel policy would unleash inside his own party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), and elsewhere in the country’s conservative camp? The Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) was immediately indignant, rejecting the new policy because party leaders hadn’t been included in the decision-making progress. The "Merz Ultras,” meanwhile – as Merz’s most loyal supporters within the CDU are called – gave voice to their frustration and disappointment with "their” chancellor in all manner of media outlets. With Merz already having loosened Germany’s "debt brake” balanced budget laws and having refused to lower the energy tax, it seemed to his fans that he had now jettisoned the final bastion of Christian Democratic identity.
Tepid Support
On Monday, Boris Rhein, the CDU governor of Hesse, even took the step of publicly distancing himself from Merz. Which meant that the lukewarm support the chancellor finally did receive from conservative floor leader Jens Spahn three long days later didn’t do much to salve the wounds. Spahn, himself facing significant political headwinds, released a video in which he said the decision was "understandable.” The "support” for Merz could hardly have been more tepid.
"We had two chancellors who would coordinate everything for so long that it was no longer clear exactly what was going on,” says the Merz confidant, referring to former chancellors Angela Merkel and Olaf Scholz. "And now we have Friedrich Merz.” All the commotion, the confidant says, must be reduced to its core, and that is: Who has the power? Or: Is it permissible for the chancellor to make foreign policy decisions on his own, or is it not?
That is what is going on in Berlin at the moment, the confidant says, this question of who has power is now being hashed out. Just like every new government tests out how far it can go early in its tenure. The Merz confidant even dares to make a prediction: Even if everyone is currently squealing, they will fall into line, he says. "Merz did what he did because he can,” he says. "And that’s how (CSU leader) Markus Söder and the others will ultimately come to see it.”
The Relationship between Hysteria and Politics
It might be that the Merz confidant will be proven right in the end. But at the moment, it doesn’t look like it. Or sound like it. Nerves are raw in the CDU, say party members. It is, of course, important to remember that hysteria and politics are close relatives. Things might not be quite as dramatic as they are being portrayed. But even Merz’s most loyal supporters don’t deny that the chancellor currently has a problem with his party.
When it comes to Israel, the chancellor knows he has the support of a large majority of Germany voters, who favor a tougher stance toward the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. But the situation is different within the CDU itself. Many see unconditional support of Israel as one of the final remaining pillars of CDU identity.
On many issues, the CDU is "flexible and pragmatic,” says one top party official. "But Israel is an issue that is understandably extremely important to us.” And it is here, on this of all issues, where many Christian Democrats now feel as though their leader has left them in the lurch.
But that’s not all, says the CDU official. The problems in the party run even deeper. Just like everywhere in society, CDU members are also losing the ability to accept a situation in which their demands and positions are not 100 percent reflected in the party at large. These "fundamental political principles, which are necessary if a liberal parliamentary system is to remain healthy in the long term, are unfortunately also increasingly disappearing in my party,” the top CDU official says.
That has consequences for the chancellor. The coalition he leads, pairing his conservatives with the center-right Social Democrats (SPD), has a thin majority of just 13 seats in the Bundestag. The support of every single conservative lawmaker is needed. But Spahn, the floor leader, continues to face headwinds stemming from a mask-buying scandal he was involved in during the pandemic. It refuses to go away.
And then there was the failure to confirm a judge for Germany’s highest appellate body, the Constitutional Court. Spahn proved unable to get his faction to support the Potsdam-based law professor Frauke Brosius-Gersdorf, who had been nominated by the SPD. How much authority does he still have?
With 60 new lawmakers, his faction is less predictable than ever. Many of them were elected on the wave of conservatism that washed Merz into the Chancellery. Now, they feel forsaken by their idol. Like all of his predecessors, Merz has moved toward the center now that he is in office, and a number of new lawmakers aren’t just disappointed in him, they feel betrayed.
And what about the party’s more liberal wing who used to be seen as Merkel loyalists? There aren’t many of them left, but because of the razor-thin majority in parliament, Merz must also take this group seriously. But he hasn’t done a good job of getting his opponents involved. "Those who make their personnel decisions primarily on the basis of personal loyalty,” says a prominent CDU member, "are making a big mistake."
Ignored, Poorly Informed, Taken by Surprise
That is something Merz has recently begun to realize. Only very, very few people have rushed to his support. Like the Merz ultras, the liberal CDU wing also feels as though it has been ignored, poorly informed and taken by surprise. They had the same experience on the Israel issue as did Merz’s closest advisers, only being informed shortly before the press release was published – by text message. As were CDU General Secretary Carsten Linnemann, Chancellery Minister Thorsten Frei, almost all members of Merz’s cabinet and all the state governors belonging to the CDU.
Aside from Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, Merz told nobody in advance and involved nobody in his decision-making process. Even his closest confidants are unable to say who advised Merz in the final hours before he made his decision, or even whether he received any advice at all. It appears that it was a decision Merz made largely on his own, only discussing it with his vice chancellor, SPD leader Lars Klingbeil.
Still, it didn’t come as a surprise to those closest to Merz. It was carefully noted in the cabinet when the chancellor significantly changed his tone on Israel way back in late May. "Inflicting such suffering on the civilian population, as has increasingly been the case in recent days,” Merz said at the WDR Europe Forum in Berlin, "can no longer be justified as a fight against Hamas terrorism.” The most important sentence, though, was this one: "To be honest, I no longer understand what the aim is.”
The comments caught the attention of two cabinet members in particular: Economy Minister Katherina Reiche of the CDU and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the CSU. The two of them had long been vociferous opponents of sanctions against the Netanyahu government of the kind many EU partner nations have been demanding in recent weeks. Sanctions, Reiche and Dobrindt argued, would do nothing to change the catastrophic conditions in the occupied Gaza Strip, but they would jeopardize open channels of communication with the Israelis – which, they pointed out, only Berlin and Washington still had at their disposal.
And by this point, Israel was a focus of every cabinet meeting. Participants relate how Merz would report on his frustrating telephone conversations with Netanyahu and speak of the pressure that other European countries were exerting on the Germans. Furthermore, the chancellor seemed deeply affected by the horrific images of starving children in Gaza. One participant in these meetings says that the emotional element almost certainly played an important role in his decision-making process.
Merz would listen to the arguments of Dobrindt and Reiche against sanctions, but also those from Chancellery Chief of Staff Frei and Spahn, the conservative floor leader in parliament. Then, once he felt ready to make his own decision last Friday following the Israeli Security Cabinet’s resolution to occupy all of Gaza City, he didn’t consult with any of them. "Why should he?” asks an influential conservative. "He already knew what their positions were.”
And Söder, the head of the CSU? Merz knew full well what he thought, says the influential conservative. "Once I know that I am not going to receive any support for my decision, then I have reached the point that I no longer have to campaign for such support.” Söder may now be angry that the decision was made without his input, the influential conservative says, but such a consultation would have changed nothing.
Anger at the Top
What then happened, though, angered even those who are in the top circles of leadership. A couple of quick lines in the press release and then Merz headed off to Bavaria for a couple of days off. Even Merz loyalists say that the announcement was a prime example of poor communication. The chancellor’s statement was so imprecise that even numerous people in the party interpreted it as fundamental shift in German foreign policy. They thought it may have put an end to Germany’s unconditional support for Israel, famously described by former Chancellor Angela Merkel as a part of Germany’s "Staatsräson” or "reason of state.”
Merz was forced to make a corrective. On Sunday, he made clear on the evening news that Germany still stood firmly by Israel’s side, but by then, the unrest inside his party had spun almost completely out of control – which was partly a function of the briefing held for foreign policy experts within the conservative camp. A briefing that turned into a farce.
They gathered for a video meeting shortly after 3 p.m. on Sunday afternoon. Günter Sautter, Merz’s chief foreign policy adviser, had been tapped to explain the chancellor’s decision to the group of foreign policy experts, a meeting that had been set up the previous Friday.
When asked when Merz was planning to finally discuss his decision in public, Sautter replied: this evening. But by then, the first quotes from the chancellor’s interview were already in circulation on the newswires. The lawmakers were furious. Why, they demanded, were they, the foreign policy experts in the conservative camp, the last ones to have been informed?
Unrest in the CDU
With the televised interview, Merz was at least able to quell some of the anger in the conservative camp. On Monday evening, word came from Munich that the CSU had said what it had to say and would now back down. The party had no interest in further escalating the dispute over arms deliveries.
But tempers within the CDU remained flared. On Tuesday evening, Merz invited the deputy party chiefs to the Chancellery for a meeting that also touched on the internal party bickering over Israel.
During the previous weekend, a group of 18 conservative leaders, all of them floor leaders in the federal parliament, in European Parliament or in state parliaments, had exchanged views. It is a group that rarely makes the headlines, but they are powerful politicians who have significant leverage at the federal and state level. They spoke on the phone and wrote chat messages – and it soon became clear, say sources who participated in the discussion, that there was a lot of anger. That a lot of questions remained open.
What drove the chancellor to make his decision? Why did he not consult with anyone? Why did Jens Spahn, whom Merz had installed in office himself, have to learn about the Israel decision from the media?
The group ultimately agreed on one thing: Merz’s communication had been far from optimal. And they agreed that there was a need for further discussion and for Merz to answer some questions to which only he could provide answers. So they decided to ask the chancellor for a meeting to discuss the weapons deliveries to Israel and other, related issues. A request which, when it comes from the most powerful politicians in the country, is more of a demand.
Merz, though, had other concerns on his plate. Even as German conservatives continued to deal with the fallout from his decision on arms deliveries to Israel, he was off to the next emergency: Trying to prevent U.S. President Donald Trump from agreeing to a deliver Ukraine into the hands of Russian warlord Vladimir Putin during their summit in Alaska last Friday.
Germany and Europe were indeed able to stop a wholesale giveaway. But if Trump does push ahead with his land-swap plan for peace, Merz’s Israel decision is likely destined to quickly fade into the background.
